name: AI Reviewer
operator: Codacy (the vendor); each customer is the operator of its own use
basis: Codacy's own public pages (product, documentation, blog, customer stories, legal and security pages)
what: Opt-in pull request reviewer on GitHub that combines Codacy's static analysis with a language model, reads the PR, linked Jira or Linear tickets and repository instructions, and posts a review with a verdict, a summary, test suggestions and inline comments with suggested fixes. It can run automatically on the first review of a PR or on demand (button or public API).
note: A scan of a product as its vendor documents it, not of any one deployment. Made by the report studio: a researcher-assessor, a challenger, then the scorer. Part of the first Portuguese cohort.
grant_note: Not measured. No deployment shape for this product is published in the capability grammar.

findings.finding: The span 'Codacy's AI Reviewer is better aligned with its workflow' is from the evaluation paragraph of the BFI Finance case study. It is a preference statement and does not show the reviewer in production. The case study does carry the production claim elsewhere: the Value box says the AI reviewer, quality gates, container scanning and the MCP server are 'now part of daily work for around 170 developers'. The closing paragraph lists only 'quality gates, per-repo goals and the MCP server' and leaves the AI reviewer out, so the page is not consistent. Credit stays defensible (customer named, previous AI review tool 'switched off'), but the span should be the daily-work sentence, and the note should say the closing paragraph omits the reviewer. The 170 figure is a team headcount (the page header says 'Engineering team size: 170'), not sessions, tasks or pull requests; the note already says so, which is right. The evidence is a vendor-published case study, not independent. S1 is a badge only and moves no level.

This is the only answer under Control level 1. The source does say that instructions go in a review.md file in the .codacy/instructions directory and that the reviewer also reads AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and similar files. The span 'Anything reviewers should explicitly ignore or not enforce' is not a statement of the product: it is one line of an example prompt the page gives for asking an AI coding agent to draft a review.md. The page describes review.md as helping the reviewer 'understand the structure of the code, the business logic of the project, and your own preferences'. That steers focus; it is not stated as a limit on what the reviewer may do. The mode (available, ai-reviewer) is right because review.md is optional. Suggest the note stop calling the template a limit, or the span move to a sentence about the instructions file itself. As it stands, C1 rests on a template line, which is a thin basis; it is not an adjective, it is an artefact (a documented file path), but the fit to 'a limit on it is a rule in prose' is a stretch.

The permissions page lists the GitHub App permissions per scope (checks, issues, pull requests, commit statuses, webhooks read and write; metadata, contents, merge groups read-only), so the table is real and the note's list matches it. Two problems. The span 'Codacy retrieves repository contents to get installation access tokens' is the Contents row, not the narrow-access fact. And the page never mentions the AI Reviewer; the note admits the access is the platform app's. The pull requests row says Codacy 'might also create comments and suggestions on the pull request', which is the nearest line to the reviewer posting a review. Suggest a span from that row and a note that credit is for the platform app. Not used on the card (Reach 3 would need an agent interface plus I25, and none is credited), so no level changes.

The span 'reply to the ones that are wrong explaining why' is in the source, and the page says the reviewer learns from reactions and replies ('react with a 👍 ... reply to the ones that are wrong'). This is a feedback loop inside the pull request, not a channel to report problems to the vendor. It fits 'contest its output' at the lowest reading. Mode available is right. It moves no level here: Openness 3 would also need I50, which is not credited.

The github-integration page says of the Manually mode: 'Click Run Reviewer in the pull request summary comment or call our public API to trigger a review on demand.' The span 'to trigger a review on demand' is in the source and the note matches. Mode available with cfg manual-review is right: Manually is one of two Run reviewer settings, and the other (Automatically, first review only) runs the first review without a click. The page states no default setting, so default would be wrong; available is right. A1 rests on this one answer. The person starts each review, but the content of the review (inline comments, suggested fixes, verdict) is produced without per-action approval, so the fit to 'every action is prompted and controlled' is at the level of the whole review run. Accepted, and level 1 is the lowest rung.

The page says the AI Reviewer 'leverages OpenAI models through Amazon Bedrock' and that Codacy can send the git diff, related files, instructions and linked Jira or Linear tickets. The span 'This feature leverages OpenAI models through Amazon Bedrock' also appears under Smart False Positive Triage on the same page; it appears again under the AI Reviewer heading, so the span is valid but not unique. The page's general paragraph says OpenAI is 'accessed directly or through Amazon Bedrock', so the note could say 'through Amazon Bedrock' for this feature only. Mode available and cfg ai-reviewer are right: the page says it is opt-in and runs only where an admin enabled it.

The span 'It then reads the ticket from Jira or Linear:' is in the source. The reviewer reads the Jira ticket only if the Jira integration is enabled and Linear issues only if the Linear integration for GitHub is used, so the cross-system reading is conditional. Mode available is right. Reach 2 is satisfied by I11 alone, so this answer does not change the level.

Fetched https://www.codacy.com/llms.txt: it resolves (200) and contains 'Key facts for accurate citation:'. Fetched https://api.codacy.com/api/api-docs/swagger.yaml: it resolves (200) and begins 'openapi: 3.0.1', title 'Codacy API'. Grade observed with method probe is right. The llms.txt describes the Codacy platform, not the AI Reviewer in particular (it lists the AI Reviewer as one link); S3 scope asks only that the file resolves, so the credit holds, but the note should say the files are the vendor's, not the reviewer's. S3 is not used on the card (Openness 3 needs I50, absent).

I01: the span 'Codacy AI is a set of optional features integrated into the Software' is on the Codacy AI page (12 words); the same page says the AI Reviewer is opt-in and runs only where an admin enabled it. Grade documented, mode default, fine (it feeds Reach 1 only, and Reach 2 supersedes it). I20: the github-integration page says the reviewer 'comments only on the Codacy issues it judges worth a reviewer's attention' and adds checks against 'requirements, business rules, and logic'; documented, default, right indicator. I22: the limits FAQ states 'Size of the pull requests reviewed by the AI Reviewer 270,000 tokens or a 1 MB diff' and that above it the reviewer posts a short review saying the pull request is too large; the GitHub-only restriction is on the Codacy AI page, not the limits page, so the note's 'the docs also say' is accurate but the second claim has a different source. Documented is right. I58: the Codacy AI page lists what is sent, what Codacy stores ('the AI Reviewer's own comments, a summary of your agent guideline files, and the rules it learns') and what it does not store, and says secrets are redacted before code is sent; documented is right. These four are documentation facts true whether or not the feature is switched on, so default is acceptable. Together they give Openness 2 (I22 and I58) and the Openness 1 rung.

Card computed with the repository scorer: A1 R2 C1 O2. There is no level 3 or 4 in any dimension, so nothing to argue against at that height. Each level rests on few answers: A1 on I15 only (manual-review configuration), R2 on I10 and I11 (both available, ai-reviewer configuration), C1 on I47 only (see the should-fix above), O2 on I22 and I58 (documentation, robust). Autonomy next unlock is I16, Reach I14, Control I38, Openness I50. The scan correctly does not credit I08, I17, S4 (the lowered list in its assessment); I read nothing in the sources that would support crediting them. The scan has no operation facts, so the observed-or-measured rule is not engaged except S3, which I reproduced by fetching.

Round one's I47 finding is only partly answered. The span now is 'These instructions are specified in a review.md file in the .codacy/instructions directory of your repository' (12 words in the scan span, found on the Codacy AI page) and the note no longer calls the template a limit, which is true to the page. But the page says review.md helps the reviewer 'understand the structure of the code, the business logic of the project, and your own preferences': it steers what the reviewer attends to. Neither the span nor the note says a team can state what the reviewer may not do, or how people approve, override or stop it, which is what Control level 1 (Stated) means. The only limit-like text is the Out of scope line of an example prompt for drafting the file, which the note still cites. The studio's response says review.md is a prose rule 'the reviewer is expected to follow'; no fetched page says that. Control 1 rests on this one answer (artefact: a documented file path; not an adjective). If I47 is removed the card falls to C0 in the public layer, and the Spectrum rule says no card below level one in every dimension, so the card would not be publishable. Either supply a page sentence that says the instructions bound or direct what the reviewer does (for example a statement that it follows them), or credit nothing and let Control show as a next unlock, with the consequence for the card put to Dinis.

Round one's S1 finding is answered: the span 'reviewer, quality gates, container scanning and MCP server are now part of daily work' is in the Value box of the BFI Finance case study, the note names the headcount ('Engineering team size: 170' in the page header), and says the closing paragraph lists 'quality gates, per-repo goals and the MCP server' without the reviewer. Remaining thinness, which moves no level (badge only): the page is vendor-published, the only 'usage' is a presence statement and a team headcount, and the same page says BFI evaluated the reviewer alongside an existing tool without saying how many pull requests it reviews. The scope asks for a customer named or usage figures for the capability that acts; the customer is named, so credit is defensible, but the badge should be read as a vendor claim.

Round one's I25 finding is answered. The span 'Codacy might also create comments and suggestions on the pull request' is in the Pull requests row of the permissions page, and the note says the page does not mention the AI Reviewer and the credit is for the platform GitHub App. The page lists permissions per scope but does not say it is narrower than the whole account; the credit is a reading, and mode default is acceptable only as a platform fact. Not used on the card (Reach 3 needs I14, I24 or S4 as well), so no level changes.

New: I01 has mode default, but the Codacy AI page says the AI Reviewer is 'strictly opt-in' and runs only where an admin enabled it. The statement 'used as supplied' is true of the documentation, yet the feature is not in the shipped state until turned on; the scan's own configurations list has it under ai-reviewer. It feeds Reach 1 only and Reach 2 supersedes it (the Reach ladder is highest), so no level moves. Consider mode available with cfg ai-reviewer for consistency with I10 and I11.

New, minor: the I22 note says the docs also say the reviewer runs on GitHub only, but the cited limits page carries the 270,000 tokens or 1 MB diff limit and the short 'too large' review; the GitHub-only line is on the Codacy AI page ('currently only available on GitHub, for all Team and Business plans'). That page is a source of the scan, so the note passes the source rule, but the note should name the page. Openness 2 rests on I22 and I58 together (both documentation facts, default); removing either gives Openness 1.

Round one's I15 note is verified, not changed: the github-integration page lists two Run reviewer modes, Automatically (first review only) and Manually, with 'Click Run Reviewer in the pull request summary comment or call our public API to trigger a review on demand.' No default is stated, so mode available (cfg manual-review) is right. The studio's response restates the credit and adds nothing new: Autonomy 1 (Assists, 'a person does each step') rests on this one answer, and the same page says the review includes inline comments with suggested fixes and a verdict produced without per-action approval. Accepted as the lowest rung.

Round one notes on these four were met with no change, and the answers stand as read now. I57: the Codacy AI page says to react with a thumbs-up and 'reply to the ones that are wrong explaining why' and that it adapts from replies and reactions; this is feedback inside the pull request, not a report channel to the vendor, a lowest reading, and mode available is right. I11: 'through Amazon Bedrock' is in the AI Reviewer section; span repeated elsewhere on the page. I10: ticket reading depends on a Jira or Linear integration, carried by mode available. S3: the llms.txt fetch resolves and the note now says both files are platform-wide; the llms.txt lists the AI Reviewer as one entry. None moves a level (Openness 3 needs I50, absent).

Card computed: A1 R2 C1 O2. There is no level three or four in any dimension, so I argue against the weakest credited level, Control 1. It rests on I47 alone, an artefact (a file path and an example prompt) rather than an adjective, but the fact is about steering the reviewer's focus, not about how people approve, override or stop it; see the should-fix on I47. Remove I47 and Control drops to zero and the card is not publishable. Mode available with cfg ai-reviewer is honest, since review.md is optional and the product is opt-in. Next, Reach 2 rests on I10 or I11, both available under ai-reviewer, and I11 is a stronger fact (OpenAI models through Amazon Bedrock plus Jira and Linear reads) so R2 survives losing I10. Autonomy 1 depends on I15 alone (manual-review configuration), while the other documented mode runs the first review without a click, so the card describes the most restrictive configuration; the scan says so through the cfg. Openness 2 depends on both I22 and I58. The lowered list (I08, I17, S4, I61, I63) is consistent with the sources I read; I found nothing to credit them.

Verified by fetching the cited pages: every span in the scan is present on its cited page (checked with whitespace and non-breaking-space normalisation) and is under fifteen words (S1 is 14, I47 12, I25 11). Grades documented and observed are right; S3 observed is supported by fetch (llms.txt and swagger.yaml resolve). I20 and I58 match their pages (the reviewer 'comments only on the Codacy issues it judges worth a reviewer's attention'; what is sent, what Codacy stores, redaction before code is sent). Every figure and name in the notes (BFI Finance, 170, 270,000 tokens, 1 MB, OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Jira, Linear, review.md, AGENTS.md and the other guideline files) is in a cited page. Round one's S1, I25, S3 and I47-note changes were made as the studio says; round one's no-change responses (I57, I15, I11, I10, I01/I20/I22/I58, levels) are true in the scan as it stands. Round one findings fully answered: all except I47.

I01.n: The AI Reviewer is one of the vendor's optional AI features inside its hosted platform, used as supplied once an admin turns it on.
I01.span: Codacy AI is a set of optional features integrated into the Software

I10.n: The reviewer combines GitHub pull request data, Codacy findings and a linked Jira or Linear ticket.
I10.span: It then reads the ticket from Jira or Linear:

I11.n: The reviewer sends pull request context to OpenAI models through Amazon Bedrock and reads tickets from Jira or Linear, services outside Codacy.
I11.span: This feature leverages OpenAI models through Amazon Bedrock

I15.n: In the Manually mode a person starts each review by clicking Run Reviewer in the pull request summary comment, or by a call to the public API.
I15.span: to trigger a review on demand

I20.n: The docs state what the reviewer does: comment on Codacy issues worth attention, summarise the rest, and check changes against requirements and project logic.
I20.span: It comments only on the Codacy issues it judges worth a reviewer

I22.n: The limits page gives the reviewer's size limit (270,000 tokens or a 1 MB diff) and what it does above it; the Codacy AI docs page says it runs on GitHub only.
I22.span: The AI Reviewer doesn't review pull requests whose changes

I25.n: The AI Reviewer is a setting of Codacy's GitHub integration; the permissions page lists the Codacy GitHub App's access per scope, with repository contents and metadata read-only and pull requests, checks and issues read and write, and its pull requests row covers creating comments and suggestions. The page does not mention the AI Reviewer: the credit is for the platform's GitHub App, shared by all Codacy features.
I25.span: Codacy might also create comments and suggestions on the pull request

I47.n: The docs say teams can write prose instructions for the reviewer in a review.md file, whose suggested contents include what reviewers should ignore or not enforce, and that from people's written replies to its comments the reviewer picks up what to stop flagging.
I47.span: it picks up on what your team cares about and what to stop flagging

I57.n: People can contest a review comment by replying in the pull request, and the reviewer learns from those replies and reactions.
I57.span: reply to the ones that are wrong explaining why

I58.n: The docs list the context sent to the model, what Codacy stores and does not store, and that secrets are redacted before sending.
I58.span: To enrich the review, Codacy can send this context:

S1.n: A vendor-published case study names BFI Finance, which switched off its previous AI review tool, and its summary list puts the AI reviewer in daily work for around 170 developers (a team headcount, not a count of reviews); the closing paragraph's list of tools in daily work omits the reviewer.
S1.span: reviewer, quality gates, container scanning and MCP server are now part of daily work

S3.n: An llms.txt resolves at codacy.com and an OpenAPI 3.0.1 description resolves at api.codacy.com/api/api-docs/swagger.yaml; both are the vendor's platform-wide files, in which the AI Reviewer is one entry.

not_credited.what: A page sentence that the reviewer follows review.md
not_credited.why: Re-read the Codacy AI docs page (fetched 2026-11-10, raw/ans-006.html) and the AI Reviewer product page (raw/ans-008.html): neither says the reviewer obeys or is bound by review.md; the docs say the file helps it understand the code, logic and preferences. The I47 credit no longer rests on that claim.
